passage:
Monday: Dadi tells Pranav, nine, about Prahlad and Holika while they shape gujiyas. 'But why didn't the fire burn Prahlad?' Pranav asks. 'Because he held on to what was good,' Dadi says. Pranav frowns, thinking.
Wednesday: At school Pranav retells it to his friend Raghav, sound effects and all. Raghav says, 'At Onam we have a story too. King Mahabali comes home once a year to see if his people are happy.' 'Why only once?' 'Ask my Achan.'
Saturday: At Holi, Pranav smears green on Raghav's cheek and whispers, 'Next Onam, you tell me the whole thing. Deal?'

qa.q: What were Dadi and Pranav shaping?
qa.a: Gujiyas.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling when he frowned after Dadi's answer?
qa.a: He felt curious and a little puzzled, still thinking about why the fire didn't burn Prahlad.

qa.q: How could Dadi or Raghav's Achan keep the friends' questions going?
qa.a: Welcome the 'why' questions, tell the stories in full, and let the two friends share each other's festivals and ask more.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel when Pranav asks to hear the whole Onam story?
qa.a: Raghav would likely feel proud and happy that a friend values Raghav's festival too.

grounding: Shows a child who hears the story behind Holi, asks why, and comes away curious about both his own festival and his friend's.

passage: Gopika, you ask why your Ammamma Manjula makes payasam at Onam and also a plum cake at Christmas? Sit. When I was ten, in Kottayam, my own Ammamma told me about Mahabali every Onam while I arranged the flowers. I kept asking, 'But why did Vamana push a good king down?' She never scolded. She said, 'Good question. Keep asking.' That December my friend Mary's mother let me help stir the cake and told me about a baby born in a stable. I asked why a king would be born among cows. She laughed. 'Good question.' I went home with two stories that year, both full of whys. I still keep both.

qa.q: What did Mary's mother let young Manjula help with?
qa.a: Stir the cake.

qa.q: What was young Manjula feeling when she kept asking about Mahabali?
qa.a: She felt curious and a little troubled, wondering why a good king would be pushed down.

qa.q: Which choice by the adults in the story helped young Manjula most?
qa.a: Ammamma and Mary's mother welcomed her questions instead of scolding, so the stories became her own and her friend's festival mattered too.

qa.q: How might Mary's mother have felt when young Manjula asked about the stable?
qa.a: She seemed amused and pleased, laughing and calling it a good question, glad to share her festival.

grounding: Illustrates a child who hears the stories behind Onam and a friend's Christmas, asks why, and carries home a sense of both festivals.

passage:
At the Holi assembly in the school hall, Ms Varghese told the story of Prahlad, the boy who kept praying even when his aunt Holika carried him into the fire, and how the fire burned her instead.

Asif, ten, put up his hand. "Why didn't it burn him?"

"Because good wins, in the story," said his classmate Ira. "That's why we light the bonfire the night before."

Asif thought. "At Eid, Abbu says we remember Ibrahim trusting God even when it was hard."

Ms Varghese smiled. "Two different stories. Both about holding on to what you believe."

That evening Asif told Ammi the Prahlad story at dinner, then asked her to tell him the Ibrahim one again, properly this time.

qa.q: Who carried Prahlad into the fire, in the story?
qa.a: His aunt Holika carried him into the fire.

qa.q: What does Asif's question 'Why didn't it burn him?' show about how he felt?
qa.a: Asif was curious and intrigued, wanting to understand the story rather than just hear it.

qa.q: How did Ms Varghese help the children connect the stories?
qa.a: She respected both and named what they share, holding on to what you believe, without ranking one above the other.

qa.q: How might Ira feel explaining Holi to Asif?
qa.a: Ira probably feels proud and happy to share her festival's meaning with a classmate.

grounding: Shows a child hearing the story behind a friend's festival, asking why, and going home with a sense of both that festival and his own.

passage:
Monday: At lunch Jahnavi explained why her family was making a flower carpet all week. "It's for King Mahabali. He was so good that everyone was equal, and he comes back once a year to see us." Sabina, nine, frowned. "Why did he have to leave?"

Wednesday: Sabina asked Umma about Mahabali while they folded clothes. Umma knew the story from her own school days and told it slowly.

Thiruvonam day: Sabina went next door to help Jahnavi finish the pookalam. While they placed marigold petals, Sabina told Jahnavi about the moon-sighting before Eid, and how her whole family ran up to the terrace to look. "Next Eid, you come up with us," she said.

qa.q: Who does Jahnavi say the flower carpet is for?
qa.a: It's for King Mahabali.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling when she asked why Mahabali had to leave?
qa.a: Sabina felt curious and a little puzzled, wanting to understand why such a good king had to go.

qa.q: What helped Sabina learn the story well?
qa.a: Asking her friend and then her Umma, and joining the pookalam, so she learned by asking and doing.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi feel when Sabina invites her up for the moon-sighting?
qa.a: Jahnavi would likely feel happy and included, getting to share Sabina's festival in return.

grounding: Shows a child learning the story behind a friend's Onam by asking why, and sharing her own Eid story in return.

passage:
Imran, you asked why the family downstairs danced so much yesterday. Sit, and let old Pranav Dadu tell you what I learned at your age.

I was nine, in a village near Amritsar. My best friend Harjeet dragged me to the fields on Baisakhi morning. The wheat was gold and everyone was singing. I asked his Bapu, "Why dance for wheat?"

He laughed and handed me a sickle. "Cut one bundle, then you'll know." It took me ten minutes, and my hands blistered. "Now imagine a whole year of waiting for this," he said. "And on this day long ago, our Guru called people to stand together as equals."

That night I told my mother both stories. She said, "Now you have Harjeet's festival and your own."

So yesterday, you should have gone down and danced.

qa.q: What did Harjeet's Bapu hand young Pranav?
qa.a: He handed him a sickle.

qa.q: How did young Pranav feel after cutting one bundle?
qa.a: His hands blistered and he felt tired but newly curious, starting to see why people celebrate the harvest.

qa.q: What turning point helped young Pranav understand Baisakhi?
qa.a: Harjeet's Bapu letting him cut a bundle himself and then telling him the story of the day, instead of just answering.

qa.q: How might Harjeet's Bapu have seen the boy's question?
qa.a: He seemed amused and glad to be asked, and chose to teach by doing.

grounding: Shows a child hearing the story behind a friend's festival after asking why, and going home with a sense of both festivals.

passage: The power went out in the middle of the Holi story at the school assembly,. Himani's grandmother, who had come to tell it, kept going in the dark. "So Holika sat in the fire with little Prahlad on her lap, and the fire burned her, not him." Hafsa, nine, raised her hand though nobody could see it. "Why didn't it burn him?" "Because he was good and brave," Nani said. "Holi is about good winning." On the way home, Hafsa told Himani about Eid. "We give food to people who don't have any. Abbu says so everyone can be happy on the same day." Himani thought about it. "So both are about being good." That evening Hafsa asked Ammi if she could play Holi with Himani, and Ammi said yes.

qa.q: Who told the Holi story at the assembly?
qa.a: Himani's grandmother.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa ask why the fire didn't burn Prahlad?
qa.a: She was curious and puzzled by the story and wanted to understand its meaning.

qa.q: What did Hafsa take home from the day?
qa.a: A sense of both her own festival, Eid, and her friend's festival, Holi, with the idea that both are about being good.

qa.q: How might Himani's grandmother feel about Hafsa's question?
qa.a: She probably felt pleased that a child was listening closely enough to ask why, even in the dark.

grounding: It illustrates a child who hears a festival story, asks why, and takes home a sense of both her own and her friend's festival.
